entities.name: Alban Roe
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alban Roe (1583–1642) was an English Benedictine martyr who was executed for his Catholic faith during the Penal Laws era, beatified in 1929 and canonised in 1970 as one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. Born Bartholomew Roe in Suffolk, he was educated at Cambridge and converted to Catholicism as a young man, later joining the English Benedictine Congregation.

Roe was ordained a priest on the European continent—the only path available to English Catholics during the Penal Laws period—and returned to England on clandestine mission. He was arrested multiple times and spent many years in various English prisons, where he continued his priestly ministry among imprisoned Catholics. Between imprisonments he served on the English mission, maintaining the Catholic faith in a country where priestly ministry was treasonous.

He was finally executed by hanging, drawing, and quartering at Tyburn on 21 January 1642, alongside John Southworth. His contemporary martyrology and the testimony of witnesses to his death made him a significant figure in the story of English Catholic martyrdom. His canonisation by Paul VI in 1970 as one of the Forty Martyrs recognised him as part of the extraordinary witness of those who died rather than apostatise from Catholicism during England's Reformation period.
